Who is linked to whom?

Learning the links from data: mutual information and Chow–Liu trees
Yuwen Huang
Advanced Machine Learning and Deep Learning · HKUST (Guangzhou)
Teaching edition
→ next · ← back · F full screen · H keys
The story

Four friends toss coins, and some copy each other

Each day, four friends toss coins and write the faces in a notebook. Some friends copy another friend's face, most of the time.

We see only the notebook. Which friends copy each other?

The links are hidden; we must learn them from the notebook.

The story · last week

Last week, the links were given, and they mattered

In Lecture 6 the links were given: a line or a circle. One more link changed every answer .

Today each circle is a friend, every face is seen, and we learn the links from data.

Every answer depends on the links, so the links must be right.

The story · the problem

There are far too many maps of links to try them all

A map says which pairs are linked. Each pair is in or out, so maps multiply.

Today's question: how do we find the links without trying every map?

Four friends: try them all. Thirty friends: impossible.

Warm-up

Two ideas from earlier lectures that come back today

1. Two friends toss without looking at each other. What is the mutual information of their faces (Lecture 3)?
Answer. Zero: one face tells nothing about the other. Today it measures a link.
2. In Lecture 5, with every coin seen, how did we fit a heads chance?
Answer. We counted: heads ÷ flips. Today it fits each link of a map.

Information measures a link; counting fits it.

Today's plan

Measure, score, build, check, then go beyond trees

Four steps take us from a notebook to a map we can trust.

Objectives

By the end of today, you can do six things

1 · Measure one link · Idea

If friend 2 copies friend 1, one face predicts the other

Guess friend 2's face: fully unsure. See friend 1's face first: if 2 copies 1, the guess is much easier.

A link is strong when one face makes the other easy to guess.

1 · Measure one link · Definition

The drop in uncertainty is the mutual information

  1. Before: entropy H(X2)H(X_2)H(X2​) of friend 2's face.
  2. After: H(X2∣X1)H(X_2\mid X_1)H(X2​∣X1​), once friend 1's face is seen.
Mutual information: I(X1;X2)=H(X2)−H(X2∣X1)I(X_1;X_2)=H(X_2)-H(X_2\mid X_1)I(X1​;X2​)=H(X2​)−H(X2​∣X1​), in nats

Mutual information: how much one face tells about the other.

1 · Measure one link · Three facts

Mutual information is the distance from no link

Compare the pair's table with the no-link table: the product of each face's chances.

I(X1;X2)=∑x1,x2p(x1,x2)⋅ln⁡p(x1,x2)p(x1)⋅p(x2)=KL(p(x1,x2) ∥ p(x1)⋅p(x2))I(X_1;X_2)=\displaystyle\sum_{x_1,x_2}p(x_1,x_2)\cdot\ln\frac{p(x_1,x_2)}{p(x_1)\cdot p(x_2)}=\mathrm{KL}\big(p(x_1,x_2)\,\|\,p(x_1)\cdot p(x_2)\big)I(X1​;X2​)=x1​,x2​∑​p(x1​,x2​)⋅lnp(x1​)⋅p(x2​)p(x1​,x2​)​=KL(p(x1​,x2​)∥p(x1​)⋅p(x2​))
  1. Symmetric: 1 tells about 2 what 2 tells about 1.
  2. Never negative, like every KL divergence.
  3. Zero exactly when there is no link: the faces are independent.

Zero means no link; larger means a stronger link.

1 · Measure one link · From the notebook

From the notebook, we count each pair's table

True chances are unseen, so we count: p^(xi,xj)=n(xi,xj)/N\hat p(x_i,x_j)=n(x_i,x_j)/Np^​(xi​,xj​)=n(xi​,xj​)/N, the counted fraction.

Counted information: I^(Xi;Xj)=∑xi,xjp^(xi,xj)⋅ln⁡p^(xi,xj)p^(xi)⋅p^(xj)\hat I(X_i;X_j)=\displaystyle\sum_{x_i,x_j}\hat p(x_i,x_j)\cdot\ln\frac{\hat p(x_i,x_j)}{\hat p(x_i)\cdot\hat p(x_j)}I^(Xi​;Xj​)=xi​,xj​∑​p^​(xi​,xj​)⋅lnp^​(xi​)⋅p^​(xj​)p^​(xi​,xj​)​

Counted fractions in, counted information out.

1 · Measure one link · Idea

Copying a copy loses more: links fade along a chain

3 copies 2, who copied 1. Each copy can go wrong, so friend 3 tells less about friend 1 than friend 2 does.

The indirect pair 1–3 is weaker than both links on its way.

1 · Measure one link · Theorem A

Theorem A: information can only fade along a chain

Theorem A (data processing). If friend 3 depends on friend 1 only via friend 2 (Markov chain X1→X2→X3X_1\to X_2\to X_3X1​→X2​→X3​), then   I(X1;X3)≤I(X1;X2)  \;I(X_1;X_3)\le I(X_1;X_2)\;I(X1​;X3​)≤I(X1​;X2​) and   I(X1;X3)≤I(X2;X3)\;I(X_1;X_3)\le I(X_2;X_3)I(X1​;X3​)≤I(X2​;X3​).

an indirect pair is never stronger than a link on its path.

Proof: chain rule in both orders; friend 3 adds nothing once friend 2 is known, so I(X1;X3)≤I(X1;X2)I(X_1;X_3)\le I(X_1;X_2)I(X1​;X3​)≤I(X1​;X2​) .

Remember: indirect pairs never beat a link on their path.

1 · Measure one link · The catch

But an indirect pair can beat a weak true link

Theorem A bounds 1–3 only by 1–2 and 2–3, its own path. So 1–3 can beat 2–4, a true but weak link.

Keeping the three strongest pairs links 1–3, misses 2–4.

The strongest pairs are not the true links.

1 · Measure one link · Next

Next: score a whole map, not one pair at a time

Links must explain the notebook together: one number per map.

A tree map's score is a sum. A sum of what?
Answer. The information on its links: Theorem B, next.

Next: one number for a whole map.

2 · Score a whole map · Idea

A tree map says how every day is made

A start friend tosses. Along each link, the next friend usually writes the same face. So each of the 2⋅2⋅2⋅2=162\cdot2\cdot2\cdot2=162⋅2⋅2⋅2=16 kinds of day gets a chance.

Each tree map is a model of the notebook.

2 · Score a whole map · Definition

A tree model: one table for the start, one for each link

Start at friend 1 and follow the links 1–2, 2–3, 2–4:

2 · Score a whole map · Fitting

Each table of a tree is fitted by counting

Each row of a link's table is a coin: when friend 2 shows H, how often does friend 3? Counting fits it .

The tables that make the notebook most likely: p^(xj∣xi)=n(xi,xj)n(xi)\hat p(x_j\mid x_i)=\dfrac{n(x_i,x_j)}{n(x_i)}p^​(xj​∣xi​)=n(xi​)n(xi​,xj​)​, counted fractions

Fitting a tree needs no search: just count.

2 · Score a whole map · Definition

The score of a map: how likely it makes the notebook

A map's score: the notebook's log-likelihood per day, with counted tables p^T\hat p_{\mathcal T}p^​T​.

ℓ(T)=1N∑d=1Nln⁡p^T(x(d))\ell(\mathcal T)=\dfrac1N\displaystyle\sum_{d=1}^{N}\ln\hat p_{\mathcal T}\big(\boldsymbol x^{(d)}\big)ℓ(T)=N1​d=1∑N​lnp^​T​(x(d)), with x(d)\boldsymbol x^{(d)}x(d) the faces on day ddd

A higher score: the map explains the notebook better.

2 · Score a whole map · Theorem B

Theorem B: a tree's score is the information on its links

Theorem B (Chow and Liu). For every tree T\mathcal TT, with counted tables, ℓ(T)=∑(i,j)∈TI^(Xi;Xj)  −  ∑iH^(Xi).\ell(\mathcal T)=\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal T}\hat I(X_i;X_j)\;-\;\sum_{i}\hat H(X_i).ℓ(T)=(i,j)∈T∑​I^(Xi​;Xj​)−i∑​H^(Xi​).

information on the links, minus a part no map can change.

Insight. Compare maps by adding their links' information.

Remember: best tree = most information on its links.

The best tree is the tree closest to the notebook

  2. Exact search: the best tree is found quickly (next section).
  3. Few numbers: each non-start friend copies one parent.

2 · Score a whole map · Next

Next: which tree carries the most information?

Among all trees, find the largest total information.

Four friends have 16 trees. About how many trees do thirty friends have?
Answer. About 104110^{41}1041: 302830^{28}3028 trees, by Cayley's formula, next.

Trying every tree is hopeless; we need a rule.

3 · Build the best map · The problem

The number of trees explodes with the number of friends

Cayley's formula: mmm friends can be linked into m m−2m^{\,m-2}mm−2 different trees.

4 friends: 42=164^2=1642=16 trees. 30 friends: 3028≈2×104130^{28}\approx 2\times10^{41}3028≈2×1041 trees.

Listing trees works for four friends, never thirty.

3 · Build the best map · Idea

Greedy rule: strongest link first, but never a loop

  1. Sort the pairs by their information, strongest first.
  2. Take the next pair, unless it closes a loop.
  3. Stop at m−1m-1m−1 links: everyone is connected.

Each step is easy: compare, then check for a loop.

3 · Build the best map · Definition

Kruskal's algorithm finds a maximum spanning tree

Definition. Spanning tree: m−1m-1m−1 links joining all mmm friends, no loop. Maximum spanning tree: largest total weight (here, information). Kruskal's algorithm: the greedy rule.
Chow–Liu tree (definition): T^=arg⁡max⁡T∑(i,j)∈TI^(Xi;Xj)\hat{\mathcal T}=\arg\max_{\mathcal T}\sum_{(i,j)\in\mathcal T}\hat I(X_i;X_j)T^=argmaxT​∑(i,j)∈T​I^(Xi​;Xj​), found by Kruskal

Chow–Liu = count, measure, then Kruskal.

3 · Build the best map · Theorem C

Theorem C: the greedy rule always finds the best tree

Theorem C (Kruskal). The greedy rule returns a spanning tree with the largest total information of all spanning trees.

the strongest link always fits in some best tree.

Why: take a tree without the strongest link 1–2.

  1. Add 1–2. This makes one loop: 1–2–3.
  2. Remove another loop link, 1–3: again a tree.
  3. 1–2 is strongest, so the swap never lowers the total. Same at every step .

The strongest safe link costs nothing: greedy is exact.

3 · Build the best map · Proof, step 1 of 5

Proof idea: greedy never rules out a best tree

Claim: after every greedy step, some best tree T\mathcal TT (blue) still holds every link greedy took (green).

3 · Build the best map · Proof, step 2 of 5

Greedy takes its next link e

Greedy takes eee (magenta). If eee is already in T\mathcal TT: nothing to do. Suppose not.

3 · Build the best map · Proof, step 3 of 5

Adding e to the best tree closes one loop

T+e\mathcal T+eT+e: a tree plus one link has exactly one loop (shaded).

3 · Build the best map · Proof, step 4 of 5

The loop holds a link f that greedy could have taken

The loop crosses greedy's groups at a blue link fff (orange). Greedy could take fff, yet chose eee: w(e)≥w(f)w(e)\ge w(f)w(e)≥w(f).

3 · Build the best map · Proof, step 5 of 5

Swapping f for e never lowers the total

w(T+e−f)=w(T)+w(e)−w(f)≥w(T)w(\mathcal T+e-f)=w(\mathcal T)+w(e)-w(f)\ge w(\mathcal T)w(T+e−f)=w(T)+w(e)−w(f)≥w(T): still a best tree, now holding eee.

Swap by swap, a best tree becomes greedy's tree.

3 · Build the best map · Theorems A and C together

With exact information, greedy finds the true links

Question: with an endless notebook (exact information), does greedy find the true links?

  1. An indirect pair is weaker than its path. 1–3 is weaker than 1–2 and 2–3 (Theorem A).
  2. So greedy meets 1–2 and 2–3 first. Then 1–3 would close a loop: skipped. Same for every indirect pair.

(Needs each copy chance between ½ and 1.)

Exact information gives the true tree; real notebooks are next.

Next: a real notebook is short; can we trust its map?

Section 3 assumed exact information. Few days make each count a little off.

Two friends toss on their own, so their true information is 0. Counted from only 20 days, their information is …
Answer. Above zero, almost always: agreeing on 12 of 20 days by chance looks like a weak link.

Next: how far off can a short notebook be?

4 · Can we trust the map? · Idea

A short notebook makes unlinked friends look linked

ProblemA real notebook is short. Friends who never copy still agree on some days, by chance.We doCount the information of a pair that never copies, in many 20-day notebooks.WhyGreedy takes the largest counts; a chance count can push out a true link.
Guarantee (Wilks). If friends iii and jjj are independent, then for large NNN, 2N⋅I^(Xi;Xj)2N\cdot\hat I(X_i;X_j)2N⋅I^(Xi​;Xj​) behaves like a chi-square variable with 1 degree of freedom, whose average is 1.

chance information averages about 1/(2N)1/(2N)1/(2N).

SoChance alone gives about 1/(2N)1/(2N)1/(2N) ; with 20 days, a fake pair matches friend 4's real link in 29% of notebooks.NextDo these mistakes disappear when the notebook grows?
4 · Can we trust the map? · Theorem D

Theorem D: with enough days, the tree is right

ProblemChance counts shrink like 1/(2N)1/(2N)1/(2N), but never reach 0.We doAsk how fast the chance of a wrong tree falls as days grow.WhyIt tells us how many days a trustworthy map needs.
Theorem D (consistency). If the friends copy along a tree (each copy chance between ½ and 1, friend 1's coin not certain), the chance that the Chow–Liu tree is wrong shrinks to 0 like e−cNe^{-cN}e−cN, some c>0c>0c>0, as the days NNN grow (proofs: references).

more days, fewer wrong maps.

SoOur friends: right in 29% of notebooks with 20 days, 93% with 320, 99% with 640.NextIn a short notebook, which link goes wrong?
4 · Can we trust the map? · Which link fails

Most mistakes misplace friend 4, the weakest link

ProblemA wrong tree tells us nothing until we know where it is wrong.We doSort the wrong trees of 1000 notebooks per length by the friend misplaced.WhyThe link that fails most is the one to check first.

True tree: 2 copies 1 (7/8); 3 and 4 copy 2 (3/4, 5/8) .

Guarantee (Tan, Anandkumar, Tong, Willsky). The rate ccc of Theorem D is set by the hardest swap: a true link against the unlinked pair on its path closest to it in information.

the weakest link decides how many days we need.

SoFriend 4 copies with only 5/8, so its weak link nearly ties with the indirect pair 1–4.NextCan we refuse a link that is too weak for the days we have?
4 · Can we trust the map? · A penalty

Keep a link only if it beats what chance can produce

ProblemGreedy always adds 3 links, even when a link is only chance.We doRun greedy, but skip pairs below a threshold set above the chance level 1/(2N)1/(2N)1/(2N) .WhyA link the days cannot support does more harm than no link.
keep the link iii–jjj only if   I^(Xi;Xj)  >  ln⁡N2N\;\hat I(X_i;X_j)\;>\;\dfrac{\ln N}{2N}I^(Xi​;Xj​)>2NlnN​
Guarantee (Tan, Anandkumar, Willsky). If the threshold tN→0t_N\to0tN​→0 but N⋅tN→∞N\cdot t_N\to\inftyN⋅tN​→∞, as for tN=ln⁡N/(2N)t_N=\ln N/(2N)tN​=lnN/(2N), the chance that the learned forest is wrong goes to 0.

fake links fall away, true links stay.

SoThe threshold is the Bayesian information criterion ; skipped pairs leave a forest.NextWhy not keep every link? More links score higher.
4 · Can we trust the map? · Why a penalty

More links always raise the notebook's own score

ProblemEach link adds information, never negative (Theorem B); the full table p^\hat pp^​ scores highest .We doScore each model on new days it never saw.WhyA good map predicts new days, not only the days it learned from.
score on new days =1M⋅∑m=1Mln⁡q(new day m)=\frac1M\cdot\sum_{m=1}^{M}\ln q(\text{new day }m)=M1​⋅∑m=1M​lnq(new day m): higher is better

qqq: the model learned from the 40 days; MMM: new days.

Guarantee (Akaike). As MMM grows, the score tends to −H(p)−D(p ∥ q)-H(p)-D(p\,\|\,q)−H(p)−D(p∥q). If the model can express ppp and has kkk free numbers, the average of D(p ∥ q)D(p\,\|\,q)D(p∥q) is about k/(2N)k/(2N)k/(2N) for large NNN: full table k=15k=15k=15, tree k=7k=7k=7.

extra numbers cost about 1/(2N) each on new days.

So2000 simulated notebooks of 40 days : tree −2.39 beats full table −2.42.NextOne notebook gives one map. How sure is each link?
4 · Can we trust the map? · Resampling

Resampling the notebook shows which links are stable

ProblemOnly one 40-day notebook.We doPick 40 of our days with replacement, run greedy; repeat 1000 times.WhyLinks resting on lucky days come and go; strong links stay.

With replacement: each pick is uniform (every day 1/40) and independent; a day may repeat. This is the bootstrap.

So1–2 and 2–3: 999 and 1000 of 1000. Friend 4 agrees with friends 2, 3, 1 on 23, 23, 22 days: a near-tie, so it splits: friend 3 in 45%, friend 1 in 28%, friend 2 in 27%.NextWhy may resamples stand in for new real notebooks?
4 · Can we trust the map? · Why resampling works

Resampling our days imitates collecting new ones

ProblemWe read resamples as if they were new notebooks.We doCompare the two recipes.WhySame recipe ⇒ trustworthy shares.
Guarantee (Efron).
  1. Same recipe: NNN independent draws, from p^\hat pp^​ instead of ppp.
  2. p^→p\hat p\to pp^​→p as NNN grows (law of large numbers).

so a link's share of resamples ≈ its chance in a new notebook.

So1–2 beats its rival 1–3 clearly (35 vs 29 agreeing days): 999 of 1000. Friend 4's pairs nearly tie (23, 23, 22): these days cannot decide.NextA link is stable. But who copies whom?
4 · Can we trust the map? · Direction

The notebook shows who is linked, not who copies whom

ProblemA link says two friends are tied, not which one copies.We doWrite the same tree starting from friend 1 and from friend 4.WhyIf both give every day the same chance, no notebook can tell them apart.
p(x1)⋅p(x2∣x1)=p(x1,x2)=p(x2)⋅p(x1∣x2)p(x_1)\cdot p(x_2\mid x_1)=p(x_1,x_2)=p(x_2)\cdot p(x_1\mid x_2)p(x1​)⋅p(x2​∣x1​)=p(x1​,x2​)=p(x2​)⋅p(x1​∣x2​)
SoInformation is not causation : arrows need experiments or assumptions.NextWhat if a friend never writes in the notebook?
4 · Can we trust the map? · A hidden friend

A hidden friend makes the others look directly linked

ProblemReal notebooks rarely record everyone who matters.We doHide friend 2's column and learn from friends 1, 3, 4 .WhyFriends 1, 3, 4 agree only through friend 2. Hide friend 2, and nothing left in the notebook explains their agreement.
So1, 3, 4 look directly linked. Fix: latent tree models, tables fitted by Lecture 5's EM.NextCan the notebook still reveal the hidden friend?
4 · Can we trust the map? · Finding a hidden friend

A hidden friend leaves a fingerprint in the agreements

ProblemFriend 2 never writes; we see only 1, 3, 4.We doTurn each pair's agreement into a strength.WhyAlong a copying path, strengths multiply.
Main idea: a strength ρ\rhoρ runs from 0 (no tie) to 1 (always the same face).
Why they multiply: a link with strength ρ\rhoρ acts like this: with chance ρ\rhoρ it passes the face on; otherwise it writes a fresh fair toss. A face crosses two links only if both pass it on: chance ρ12⋅ρ23\rho_{12}\cdot\rho_{23}ρ12​⋅ρ23​ .
SoTry friend 1 as the centre: then 3 and 4 should agree less than they do. Friends 3 and 4 fail the same way. So the centre is someone we cannot see.NextCan we compute the hidden centre's links?
4 · Can we trust the map? · Finding the hidden friend, step 1 of 4

Each seen pair is a path through the hidden centre

Call the centre's three links a,b,ca,b,ca,b,c. Strengths multiply along paths: a⋅b=38,  a⋅c=316,  b⋅c=18a\cdot b=\tfrac38,\; a\cdot c=\tfrac3{16},\; b\cdot c=\tfrac18a⋅b=83​,a⋅c=163​,b⋅c=81​.

4 · Can we trust the map? · Finding the hidden friend, step 2 of 4

Multiply two equations, divide by the third

a2=(a⋅b)⋅(a⋅c)b⋅c=3/8⋅3/161/8=916a^2=\dfrac{(a\cdot b)\cdot(a\cdot c)}{b\cdot c}=\dfrac{3/8\cdot3/16}{1/8}=\tfrac9{16}a2=b⋅c(a⋅b)⋅(a⋅c)​=1/83/8⋅3/16​=169​, so a=34a=\tfrac34a=43​.

4 · Can we trust the map? · Finding the hidden friend, step 3 of 4

Dividing by a gives the other two links

b=38÷34=12,c=316÷34=14b=\tfrac38\div\tfrac34=\tfrac12,\qquad c=\tfrac3{16}\div\tfrac34=\tfrac14b=83​÷43​=21​,c=163​÷43​=41​.

4 · Can we trust the map? · Finding the hidden friend, step 4 of 4

The hidden friend's habits come back exactly

Undo the strength, P=(1+ρ)/2P=(1+\rho)/2P=(1+ρ)/2: copy chances 7/8, 3/4, 5/8, friend 2's habits.

Guarantee (Choi, Tan, Anandkumar, Willsky). If each hidden friend links at least three others, no strength 0 or ±1, the seen pairs determine the hidden tree.
SoHidden friends are findable; EM (Lecture 5) then fits their tables.NextCollect the checks before believing a map.
4 · Can we trust the map?

Before believing a map, make three checks

  1. Is each link above its penalty? If not, drop it.
  2. Does each link survive resampling? Report how often it appears.
  3. Does the map beat simpler maps on new days?

And remember: links are not arrows, and a hidden friend fakes links.

Trust a map only after these checks.

4 · Can we trust the map? · Next

Next: what if the true map has a loop?

So far: copying along a tree. Real friends may watch two.

Friend 4 copies friend 2 on some days and friend 3 on others; friend 3 copies friend 2. How many links does the true map have?
Answer. Four: 1–2, 2–3, 2–4, 3–4, with the loop 2–3–4.

Next: maps with loops, beyond trees.

5 · Beyond trees · Idea

What if friend 4 watches two friends?

ProblemReal friends may copy more than one friend; a tree cannot show that.We doEach day a fair toss picks whom friend 4 copies: friend 2 or friend 3.WhyIt is the smallest change that puts a loop into the truth.
SoFriends 2, 3, 4 now form a loop: four true links, not three.NextWhat does the tree method do with a loop?
5 · Beyond trees · The trouble

The best tree must drop a true link of the loop

ProblemA tree on four friends has exactly 3 links; the truth has 4.We doRun greedy on a perfect notebook of the loop .WhyTo see which true link a tree is forced to lose.
SoGreedy keeps 1–2, 2–4, 3–4 and drops the true link 2–3.NextWe need a test for one link that works without a tree.
5 · Beyond trees · Theorem E

No link means no information once the others are known

ProblemFriends 1 and 4 agree often, yet are not linked.We doAsk: once friends 2 and 3 are known, does friend 1 still help guess friend 4?WhyFriend 4 copies only 2 or 3, so friend 1 reaches 4 only through them.

1–4: with 2 and 3 known, friend 1 adds nothing: no link. 2–4: even with 1 and 3 known, friend 2 still helps (4 copies it on half the days): link.

Theorem E (pairwise Markov property). If every day has positive chance, iii and jjj are linked in the smallest fitting map exactly when XiX_iXi​ and XjX_jXj​ are dependent given all the other friends .

a link is a tie the other friends cannot explain.

SoTest a link given the other friends, not alone.NextHow do we measure information given other friends?
5 · Beyond trees · Definition

Conditional information measures a link given the others

ProblemPlain information of 1 and 4 also counts their tie through 2 and 3.We doSort days into piles by the faces of 2 and 3; measure 1–4 inside each pile; average.WhyInside a pile, 2 and 3 never change, so they cannot carry a tie: what is left is direct.
I(X1;X4∣X2,X3)=∑piles(share of days)⋅(information of 1, 4 inside the pile)I(X_1;X_4\mid X_2,X_3)=\displaystyle\sum_{\text{piles}}(\text{share of days})\cdot(\text{information of 1, 4 inside the pile})I(X1​;X4​∣X2​,X3​)=piles∑​(share of days)⋅(information of 1, 4 inside the pile)
SoIt is zero exactly when no pile shows a tie: 1 and 4 need no link. Any friends SSS work the same way.NextWhat does sorting into piles cost?
5 · Beyond trees · The cost

Conditioning on many friends needs many days

ProblemGiven all m−2m-2m−2 other friends, the days split into 2m−22^{m-2}2m−2 groups.We doCount how many days each group keeps.WhyA group with few days gives large chance counts again .
SoWilks again, with one degree of freedom per group: chance gives about (groups) ÷ (2N) : condition on as few friends as possible.NextA method that tests with small groups first.
5 · Beyond trees · Method 1: test the links

Test each link, and remove it when a few friends explain it

ProblemTesting given all others needs too many days.We doThe PC algorithm (for Peter Spirtes, Clark Glymour): start with all six links; test given no friend, then one, then two.WhyIf any set of friends explains a tie, the link is not needed; small sets need few days.
Guarantee (Spirtes, Glymour; Kalisch, Bühlmann). If every independence of ppp shows in its map (faithfulness) and every test is right, the PC algorithm returns the true links; as NNN grows, the tests are right with chance tending to 1.
SoThe four true links remain, loop included.NextOr judge whole maps at once, as with trees?
5 · Beyond trees · Method 2: score and search

Or score every map, and search by small moves

ProblemPC decides one link at a time; one wrong test spoils the map.We doGive each whole map one score, then climb.WhyFit alone always prefers more links ; the penalty stops that.
  1. Score = fit to the notebook − a cost for each extra number .
  2. Start from the Chow–Liu tree.
  3. Try every one-link change; take the best if the score rises; stop when none does.
SoOn the loop, one move adds the missing link 2–3. Cost: with a loop, scoring needs inference (Lecture 6), not counting.NextDoes the climb find the best map?
5 · Beyond trees · Theorem F

Theorem F: finding the best map with loops is hard

ProblemOne-link moves can stop where no single move helps.We doAsk whether any fast method finds the best map.WhyIf none does, we must accept good maps, not best ones.
Theorem F (Chickering). Finding the highest-scoring map with arrows is NP-hard, even with at most two parents per friend.

beyond trees, the climb may stop only locally best.

Guarantee (Chickering, 2002). Climb in two phases: first only add links while the score rises, then only remove links while it rises. With enough days and a faithful ppp , the climb ends at the true map (arrows only as far as data can show them ).
SoWorst case: no fast method is known to find the best score. Yet with enough days, the two-phase climb ends at the truth. Trees: greedy is always exact (Theorem C) .NextCan loops at least show us arrows?
5 · Beyond trees · A collider

Two unlinked friends become linked given a third

ProblemLinks alone never show arrows .We doLet friends 2 and 3 toss alone; friend 4 copies one of them.WhyTwo causes meeting in one friend behave unlike a chain.
SoUnlinked alone, linked given friend 4: explaining away.NextDoes this pattern reveal the arrows?
5 · Beyond trees · Theorem G

A collider shows the arrows: both point into friend 4

ProblemWhich arrows can any notebook see?We doCompare chain, fork and collider on three friends.WhyOnly shapes that give different chances can be told apart.
Theorem G (Verma and Pearl). Two arrow maps give the same models exactly when they share links and colliders (two arrows into one friend from unlinked friends).

colliders are the arrows the data can see.

SoA chain or a fork hides its arrows; a collider shows them.NextCollect Part 1, then run every step on the friends' notebook.

Example · All six pairs

All six pairs: one indirect pair beats a true link

Each friend shows H half the time, so the same-face count gives the information . Same face: 1–2 on 448, 2–3 on 384, 1–3 on 352, 2–4 on 320, 1–4 on 304, 3–4 on 288 days.

Example · Greedy rule · Step 1 of 4

Step 1: friends 1 and 2 share the most, so we link them

The strongest pair, 1–2 (0.316), cannot close a loop: there are no links yet.

Link 1–2.

Example · Greedy rule · Step 2 of 4

Step 2: friends 2 and 3 come next, and no loop forms

Pair 2–3 (0.131) joins friend 3 to the group of friends 1 and 2.

Example · Greedy rule · Step 3 of 4

Step 3: friends 1 and 3 would close a loop, so we skip

Pair 1–3 (0.072) is strongest left, but 1 and 3 are already connected through 2. It would close loop 1–2–3, where it is weakest (Theorem A).

Skip 1–3: the loop check catches the indirect pair.

Example · Greedy rule · Step 4 of 4

Pair 2–4 (0.032) joins friend 4. With 3=4−13=4-13=4−1 links everyone is connected, so pairs 1–4 and 3–4 are not needed.

The learned tree is the true tree: 1–2, 2–3, 2–4.

Example · A collider

A collider: 2 and 3 are unlinked until friend 4 is known

ProblemFriends 2 and 3 toss alone; friend 4 copies one of them (chance 7/8).We doGuess friend 3's face from friend 4, then learn friend 2 too.WhyIf learning 2 changes our guess about 3, they are linked given 4.
  1. Friend 4 wrote H. Friend 3 wrote H on 88 of those 128 days: 0.69.
  2. Also friend 2 wrote T. Then 4's H likely came from 3: friend 3 H on 32 of 40 days, 0.8.
SoFriend 2 explains away part of 4's H: given 4, 2 and 3 are linked (conditional information 0.014) .NextThe same question inside today's AI.
Part 2 · Next

Next: the same question inside today's AI

Friends become words, records, balls or variables; the question stays: who is linked to whom?

A language model links each word to other words. How often does it choose these links?
Answer. Anew for every sentence: attention, the last slide of Part 3.

Learning links is everywhere in machine learning.

Part 3 · In AI today

Learning links runs inside many systems

Only the friends change: words, records, particles, variables.

Part 3 · Classifiers

A spam filter can link words that appear together

  1. Friends = words of an email; notebook = emails marked spam or not.
  2. Naive Bayes: words unlinked given the class, so "free" and "money" count twice.
  3. Tree-augmented naive Bayes adds a Chow–Liu tree on the words, using information given the class.

One extra tree of links, and evidence is no longer counted twice.

Part 3 · Mixtures of trees

When one tree is not enough, EM mixes several trees

  1. Records follow different maps: a hidden choice of tree, like Lecture 5's hidden coin; fit it with Lecture 5's expectation–maximization (EM).
  2. Guess step: soft labels say which tree made each record.
  3. Count step: Chow–Liu per tree, weighted by the soft labels.

Lecture 5's EM plus today's Chow–Liu: a mixture of trees.

Part 3 · Physics from motion

A neural network learns which balls are tied by springs

  1. Friends = moving balls; notebook = their trails.
  2. Links = hidden springs. One network guesses them; a second predicts the motion.
  3. Both train on Lecture 6's evidence lower bound, with links as hidden variables.

Neural relational inference learns the links with Lecture 6's score.

Part 3 · Learning arrows

One equation forbids loops, so gradients can learn arrows

ProblemSearching arrow maps one move at a time is slow and can stop early (Theorem F).We doWrite the map as weights WWW (Wij≠0W_{ij}\neq0Wij​=0: arrow i→ji\to ji→j); turn "no loop of arrows" into one equation.WhyThen gradient descent, as for neural networks, searches all maps at once.
no loop of arrows   ⟺  h(W)=tr⁡(eW∘W)−m=0\iff h(W)=\operatorname{tr}\big(e^{W\circ W}\big)-m=0⟺h(W)=tr(eW∘W)−m=0

W∘WW\circ WW∘W: squared entries; (W∘W)k(W\circ W)^k(W∘W)k has a positive diagonal entry exactly when a loop of length kkk exists; eA=I+A+A2/2!+⋯e^{A}=I+A+A^2/2!+\cdotseA=I+A+A2/2!+⋯ adds all lengths; tr⁡\operatorname{tr}tr sums the diagonal. No loop: diagonal of eAe^AeA is all 1, trace =m=m=m friends.

SoNOTEARS: maximize fit − penalty subject to h(W)=0h(W)=0h(W)=0. A good map, not always the best; arrows still need assumptions (e.g. equal noise).NextCan links change with every input?
Part 3 · Coming in Week 13

Attention chooses new links for every sentence

  1. Friends = words of one sentence.
  2. Each word weights every (earlier) word: a soft map, computed anew for each sentence.
  3. Today: one map per notebook. Attention learns how to draw a map per input.

From one learned map to a new map for every input.

Summary · The whole story

From a notebook to a map of links we can trust

Who copies whom? We see only the notebook; maps are too many to try.

  1. Measure each pair: mutual information, zero for no link.
  2. Score a tree: the information on its links (Theorem B).
  3. Build the best tree: strongest first, never a loop (Theorem C).
  4. Check it: penalty, resampling, new days.
  5. Beyond trees: test a link given the others; colliders show arrows.

On a tree, data give links, not arrows; a hidden friend fakes links.

Measure, score, build, check.

Check yourself

Check yourself (1 of 3): measuring and building

1. Two friends' counted information over 30 days is 0.02. Are they linked?
Answer. Not necessarily: chance alone gives about 1/(2N)≈0.0171/(2N)\approx0.0171/(2N)≈0.017.
2. Pair 1–3 has more information than pair 2–4, yet the greedy rule skips 1–3. Why?
Answer. It closes a loop 1–2–3, whose other links are stronger.

Chance makes links look real; loops reveal indirect pairs.

Check yourself

Check yourself (2 of 3): scores and arrows

3. We join two separate pieces of a map with one more link. The notebook's score …
Answer. Never falls: it rises by the link's information, so we need a penalty.
4. Can the notebook tell whether friend 2 copies friend 1, or friend 1 copies friend 2?
Answer. No: both starting friends give every day the same chance.

More links always fit better; on a tree, arrows need an experiment.

Check yourself

Check yourself (3 of 3): beyond trees

5. Friends 1 and 4 have information 0.09 between them, yet need no link. How can that be?
Answer. Given friends 2 and 3 it is 0: they carry all the news between 1 and 4.
6. Friends 2 and 3 are independent, but dependent once friend 4 is known. Which arrows does this show?
Answer. 2 → 4 ← 3: a collider, the arrows the data can see.

Test links given the others; colliders show arrows.

Appendix · Measure · Proof

Proof of Theorem A: count the same information two ways

Chain rule (Lecture 3): what two faces tell together = what the first tells + what the second adds given the first. Markov chain: once x2x_2x2​ is known, x3x_3x3​ tells nothing more about x1x_1x1​.

I(X1;X2,X3)=I(X1;X2)+I(X1;X3∣X2)=I(X1;X2)I(X_1;X_2,X_3)=I(X_1;X_2)+I(X_1;X_3\mid X_2)=I(X_1;X_2)I(X1​;X2​,X3​)=I(X1​;X2​)+I(X1​;X3​∣X2​)=I(X1​;X2​)
chain rule; the last term is 0 on a chain
I(X1;X2,X3)=I(X1;X3)+I(X1;X2∣X3)I(X_1;X_2,X_3)=I(X_1;X_3)+I(X_1;X_2\mid X_3)I(X1​;X2​,X3​)=I(X1​;X3​)+I(X1​;X2​∣X3​)
chain rule, in the other order
I(X1;X3)=I(X1;X2)−I(X1;X2∣X3) ≤ I(X1;X2)I(X_1;X_3)=I(X_1;X_2)-I(X_1;X_2\mid X_3)\ \le\ I(X_1;X_2)I(X1​;X3​)=I(X1​;X2​)−I(X1​;X2​∣X3​) ≤ I(X1​;X2​)
subtract; information is never negative

The chain read backwards, X3→X2→X1X_3\to X_2\to X_1X3​→X2​→X1​, is also a Markov chain, so the same steps give I(X1;X3)≤I(X2;X3)I(X_1;X_3)\le I(X_2;X_3)I(X1​;X3​)≤I(X2​;X3​). Our friends: 1 and 3 show the same face when both copies are right or both wrong: 78⋅34+18⋅14=1116\tfrac78\cdot\tfrac34+\tfrac18\cdot\tfrac14=\tfrac{11}{16}87​⋅43​+81​⋅41​=1611​, information 0.072, below 0.131 and 0.316.

Given the middle friend, the far friend adds nothing, so information cannot grow.

Appendix · Beyond trees · Details

Theorem E needs every day to have a positive chance

Theorem E combines the pairwise Markov property with the Hammersley–Clifford theorem: for a positive model, the pairs dependent given all others are exactly the links of the smallest fitting map.

Why positivity matters: let three friends always write the same face. Given any one of them, the other two are fixed, so every pair is independent given the third, and the test removes every link, though the faces are tied together.

In our friends every day has a positive chance (no copy is certain), so the test is safe.

With certain copies, conditional tests can erase real links.
